query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing rhenium (Re) into equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW to form Nb20Mo20Ta20W20Re20 will enhance room‐temperature ductility and irradiation resistance while preserving its excellent high‐temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, single-BCC-phase, columnar nanocrystalline Nb25Mo25Ta25W25 refractory high-entropy alloy films produced by magnetron sputtering onto Si(111).
generation.intervention: Incorporate Re to create an equiatomic NbMoTaWRe alloy (Nb20Mo20Ta20W20Re20) via magnetron sputtering under identical conditions.
generation.conditions: Films prepared at room temperature under controlled Ar atmosphere (approx. 5.0 × 10^-1 Pa) and base pressure (~6.0 × 10^-4 Pa), followed by 120 keV He2+ irradiation at a fluence of 1×10^16 ions/cm^2 (dose rate 1×10^13 ions/cm^2/s) at room temperature; damage confined to an approximately 400 nm region as estimated by SRIM.
generation.structural_mediator: Re addition refines the grain structure, increases lattice distortion and excess free volume, and produces several-nanometer-wide amorphous regions at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: These structural modifications create additional defect-sink sites that enhance the annihilation of irradiation-induced vacancies, thereby suppressing the growth and segregation of He-bubbles along grain boundaries. This is expected to reduce irradiation-induced hardening and boundary embrittlement, while the refined grain structure improves ductility at room temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to Re-free Nb25Mo25Ta25W25 films, Nb20Mo20Ta20W20Re20 films will display smaller and more uniformly dispersed He bubbles, less irradiation-induced hardening, and improved room-temperature ductility. High-temperature performance is predicted to remain excellent due to retention of the BCC structure.
generation.baseline: The Re-free Nb25Mo25Ta25W25 films under identical deposition and irradiation conditions serve as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits apply under room temperature conditions and for irradiation using 120 keV He2+ (fluence 1×10^16 ions/cm^2) within the ~400 nm irradiated region. Extrapolation to other temperatures or irradiation conditions requires further validation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in ductility and irradiation resistance, and the potential influence of Re on high-temperature mechanics, remain uncertain and warrant additional investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of films—one of pure NbMoTaW and one of NbMoTaWRe—using identical magnetron sputtering parameters on Si(111). Subject both sets to 120 keV He2+ irradiation at room temperature with a fluence of 1×10^16 ions/cm^2. Analyze the microstructure pre- and post-irradiation using cross-sectional TEM (including FFT analyses to assess grain size, lattice distortion, and amorphous boundary layers), XRD (for phase confirmation), and measure the mechanical properties using nanoindentation (load-displacement curves) and in situ micropillar compression tests.
measurements: Grain size and distribution via TEM/FFT
Presence and distribution of amorphous interfacial regions
He bubble size and spatial uniformity
Nanoindentation load-displacement curves indicating irradiation hardening
In situ micropillar compression results indicating ductility and boundary embrittlement
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NbMoTaWRe films do not show significantly smaller, more uniformly distributed He bubbles, or if they exhibit similar or greater irradiation-induced hardening and reduced ductility compared to NbMoTaW films, then the hypothesis that Re addition improves room-temperature irradiation tolerance and ductility would be rejected.
